questions.question: Which statement is TRUE about the JVM's method area (Metaspace in Java 8+)?
options: It stores class metadata, static variables, and the constant pool
It stores local variables and method call frames
It is garbage collected using the same GC cycle as the heap
Each thread has its own private method area
questions.answer: It stores class metadata, static variables, and the constant pool

questions.question: A class declares: 'private final int x;' without initialization. What is the result?
options: Compile-time error: blank final field x may not have been initialized
x defaults to 0 only if initialized in a static block
Runtime NullPointerException when x is accessed
questions.answer: Compile-time error: blank final field x may not have been initialized

options: Dog.sound() is called at runtime via dynamic dispatch

questions.question: In Java, why can an interface have 'default' methods since Java 8?
options: To allow adding new methods to interfaces without breaking existing implementing classes
To allow interfaces to have constructors for default initialization
To replace abstract classes entirely in the Java type system
To allow default methods to be called without an object reference
questions.answer: To allow adding new methods to interfaces without breaking existing implementing classes

questions.question: Which statement correctly explains 'island of isolation' in Java garbage collection?
options: A group of objects that reference each other but are not reachable from any GC root
A single object with no references at all
An object whose only reference is from a static field
An object that holds a reference to itself
questions.answer: A group of objects that reference each other but are not reachable from any GC root

questions.question: What is the difference between 'throws' and 'throw' in Java exception handling?
options: 'throw' raises an exception instance; 'throws' declares exceptions a method may propagate
'throws' raises an exception instance; 'throw' declares exceptions a method may propagate
'throw' is for checked exceptions only; 'throws' is for unchecked exceptions only
Both keywords are interchangeable in Java 8+
questions.answer: 'throw' raises an exception instance; 'throws' declares exceptions a method may propagate

s1 == s2 is true; s1 == s3 is true; s1.equals(s3) is true

questions.question: Which statement about Java's 'volatile' keyword is TRUE?
options: volatile guarantees visibility of changes across threads but does NOT guarantee atomicity of compound actions
volatile makes a variable immutable and thread-safe for all operations
volatile is equivalent to using synchronized on the variable
volatile forces the JVM to store the variable on the stack instead of heap
questions.answer: volatile guarantees visibility of changes across threads but does NOT guarantee atomicity of compound actions

questions.question: In Java generics, what does the wildcard '? extends Number' allow?
options: Reading elements as Number; writing is prohibited (except null)
Writing any subtype of Number; reading returns Object
Reading and writing any subtype of Number freely
Restricting the generic type to exactly Number, no subtypes
questions.answer: Reading elements as Number; writing is prohibited (except null)

questions.question: What happens when serialization encounters a field marked 'transient'?
options: The field is skipped during serialization and gets its default value upon deserialization
The field causes a NotSerializableException to be thrown
The field is serialized normally but marked with a special flag
The field retains its last value upon deserialization via object caching
questions.answer: The field is skipped during serialization and gets its default value upon deserialization
